@@ -762,6 +762,7 @@ everything target-specific is independent.
 | D60 | An ALL-CAPS reference is checked against the document's real declared token set, not just its spelling | **`Diagnostics.undefinedNonterminals`/`checkDefined` gain a `declaredTokens: Set[String]` parameter — the document's own `## Tokens` block, parsed for real by `Tokens.parseTokens` and threaded through from `Lr.parseWith` (which already has the raw markdown to hand). When `declaredTokens` is non-empty, an ALL-CAPS reference that isn't among them is now a new, real diagnostic — `` undefined token class `X` `` — with a did-you-mean against the other declared tokens, mirroring the existing undefined-nonterminal check exactly. When `declaredTokens` is empty (the document has no `## Tokens` block at all — lexer-spec.md §6's whole-grammar "external mode", where the entire scanner is supplied out of band, e.g. `examples/readme.gram.md`'s `WORD`), an ALL-CAPS reference is left unchecked, exactly as before D60. The pre-existing spelling-based `terminalLikeRefs` heuristic survives only as the did-you-mean fallback for that external-mode case, where no real declared set exists to suggest from.** | Closes a real, previously-silent gap: a typo'd ALL-CAPS reference in a grammar that already declares its own tokens locally (the common case — most shipped examples) was never checked against anything and was silently treated as "presumably a valid terminal", the exact opposite of the mixed-case undefined-nonterminal check two lines above it in the same function, which has always been a hard error. `unusedTokenWarnings` (a declared-but-unreferenced token, the other direction of the same typo) already existed; this adds its missing complement. Scoped to only fire when the document has actually declared something locally, rather than unconditionally, because `## Tokens` is genuinely optional (whole-grammar external mode) and a real, checked-in example (`readme.gram.md`) depends on that leniency. |
 | D61 | `Tokens.validateName`'s ALL-CAPS requirement stays a hard gate; round-trip fidelity is solved by `@spelling("...")` instead | **Investigated relaxing the ALL-CAPS-only requirement on a declared token's name to a lint (in response to a request to support importing non-ALL-CAPS names, e.g. ANTLR's `Digit` — ANTLR only requires an uppercase FIRST letter, not the whole word). Found it can't be relaxed in isolation: `Lr.classifyFenceContent`'s fence-role self-identification ("case is law", D-grammar-roles) requires *every* line in a `## Tokens` fence to independently look ALL-CAPS-before-`:` to be recognized as a Tokens fence at all; a lowercase-named line would silently fall through to `FenceKind.Rule` instead (and, post-D59, a single-line rule head is now `IDENT : ... ;`-shaped too — textually identical to a token definition line for a name that isn't ALL-CAPS). So the requirement is structural, not stylistic, and stays exactly as strict as before. Instead, `TokenDef`/`IRTokenClass` gain an optional `nativeSpelling: Option[String]` (the `@spelling("...")` modifier, parsed by `Tokens.scala`'s own hand-rolled, non-bootstrap parser — no self-hosting/production-id risk): `ConvertAntlr` renames a non-ALL-CAPS ANTLR lexer rule (`Digit` → `DIGIT`) and records the original via `@spelling("Digit")`, rewriting every parser-rule reference to the same renamed name (`renderAtom`'s `rename` map) so nothing dangles; `BackendAntlr` re-emits under the recorded original spelling when present, not Gramaire's internal ALL-CAPS name.** | The real, underlying need from the debate that prompted this (round-trip fidelity with ANTLR/Bison/EBNF, none of which share Gramaire's case convention) doesn't actually require relaxing Gramaire's own authoring format — it requires Gramaire to *remember* an import's original spelling. `@spelling` delivers exactly that, safely, without touching fence classification, the self-hosting bootstrap, or any existing golden fixture (the field is optional and omitted from JSON when absent, following the same convention as `sourceLayout`/`diagramView`/`name`, D56/D58). Rejected: relaxing `classifyFenceContent` to accept non-ALL-CAPS Tokens lines too — that would need a *new* disambiguation mechanism (contradicting D-grammar-roles' "no keyword, ever" stance) to replace the one case-based signal removes, for no benefit `@spelling` doesn't already provide. |
 | D62 | A renamed nonterminal's original spelling round-trips via a `<Name>.gramaire-names.json` sidecar, never an in-band `.g4` comment | **The matching hazard on the opposite side of the ANTLR converter from D61: `BackendAntlr.ruleName` force-lowercases a nonterminal's first letter on export (`Expr` → `expr`), because a real ANTLR parser rule can never start uppercase (that's always a lexer rule in ANTLR, not a style choice — unlike D61's tokens, this can never arise on IMPORT, since any real ANTLR parser rule name is already lowercase-initial by ANTLR's own hard requirement). The hazard is real only in the `emit --backend antlr` → hand-edit → `import` workflow the CLI advertises side by side: without a fix, Gramaire's own capitalized house style (`Expr`, `Term`) silently and permanently becomes lowercase on that round trip. A first pass recorded the original name as an in-band `// @gramaire-name: Expr` comment in the exported `.g4` itself — rejected on review: ANTLR's own file format isn't Gramaire's to annotate, and it's the one export among all of Gramaire's backends that would carry a Gramaire-specific marker a plain ANTLR toolchain has no reason to understand. Replaced with `BackendAntlr.renameMap(ir): Map[String, String]` (ANTLR name → original Gramaire name, only for rules actually renamed) written to a **separate sidecar file**, `<Name>.gramaire-names.json`, alongside the plain, unannotated `.g4` — the `Backend.emit` `Vector[Output]` shape (already multi-file-capable) needed no changes to carry it. `ConvertAntlr.importAntlr` gained an optional `renameMap` parameter (default empty) it threads into the *same* `rename` map D61's `lexerRename` already passes through `renderTopAlt`, so every reference to a restored rule — not just its own heading — comes back consistently; `ConvertAntlr.parseRenameMap` decodes the sidecar's JSON, and the CLI's `import` command (`renameMapSidecarOf`) looks for and reads it automatically next to the `.g4` being imported, falling back to `Map.empty` (silently, not an error) when no sidecar exists — the common case for any hand-written ANTLR grammar, or a `.g4` Gramaire exported but renamed nothing in.** | Confirms and closes the exact gap Marcus/Devon named in the original ANTLR-vs-Gramaire debate ("a workflow the CLI literally advertises side-by-side") without polluting an output format Gramaire is a guest in — the `.g4` a `gramaire emit --backend antlr` user hands to a colleague, or feeds into a real `antlr4` toolchain, reads as completely ordinary ANTLR, with the provenance living in a file only Gramaire's own `import` ever needs to look for. Mirrors `.gram.lock`'s own established sidecar convention (a derived, drift-checkable artifact living beside its source) rather than inventing a second in-band-comment mechanism alongside D61's real-syntax `@spelling(...)` modifier (which stays as is: it extends *Gramaire's own* Tokens format, not someone else's). |
+| D63 | Heading lines split out of a `.gram.md` prose gap into their own Notebook cell, Livebook-style | **A `.gram.md` document's markdown gaps (the text between/around `` ```gramaire `` fences) used to collapse into exactly one "prose" `DocBlock` regardless of how much structure they held — a `## Term` heading, several paragraphs, an image, all fused into one big click-to-edit textarea. `document.ts`'s `buildDocument` now takes an injected `splitProse` callback (the same injection pattern `sectionEndIndex`'s own `headingLevelOf` already uses, keeping this module markdown-agnostic per its own header) that further divides each gap into a new `"heading"` `DocBlockKind` (one `#`/`##`/`###` line, `headingLevel: 2 \| 3 \| 4`) and the `"prose"` runs between them. `markdown.ts`'s new `splitHeadingsFromProse` is the real implementation `GramaireNotebookIsland.tsx` supplies, sharing the exact same heading regex `parseMarkdownLite` already matches against; its descriptors always join back to the original gap text byte-for-byte, so no content is ever silently dropped, only reattributed to a different sibling block than before. A real local Livebook instance was fetched and inspected as UX reference during design: Livebook's own model is that a heading defines a section boundary and is itself a separately addressable element, while the body underneath (paragraphs, images, tables) stays one shared unit — the user explicitly confirmed this coarser scope over a more aggressive per-paragraph/per-table split. `headingLevelOf` (the callback `sectionEndIndex`/`moveBlock` need for Livebook-style section-aware reordering, which already existed for the old "first heading inside a bigger prose block" case) simplifies from a `parseMarkdownLite`/`leadingHeading` re-parse to a direct `block.headingLevel` field read; moving a heading cell now moves its own trailing content along with it via that same, unmodified mechanism — the user's own explicit requirement, verified end-to-end against a real multi-heading document (not just the pre-existing generic stub-driven tests). `isPaperBlock` widens to include `"heading"` so Paper view/PDF export keep showing every heading. Re-splitting a gap only ever happens at `buildDocument` time — the existing debounced-reshape-after-`scheduleEvaluate` flow, never synchronously on every keystroke — the same rule that already governs every other structural change in this file, for the same OOM-avoidance reason its own header comments document; a heading typed mid-edit inside an existing prose cell renders correctly immediately (embedded headings already render inline) and only splits into its own cell once the next reshape lands.** | The literal ask — "like Gramaire fences are separate live-edit elements, each different markdown cell should be scoped" — needed a real UX reference to size correctly: a naive reading could have meant splitting every paragraph and table into its own cell too, a much larger, more invasive change with no analogue in the reference the user actually pointed at. Fetching and inspecting a real Livebook instance resolved that ambiguity concretely rather than guessing, and confirming the narrower scope with the user before implementing kept the change small — no new synchronous re-split machinery, no new `"table"` kind, just one new block kind riding the SAME injected-callback, debounced-reshape, and section-move mechanisms this file already had for its other markdown-agnostic concerns. |
